passage:
At two, Jomon ran laps round the living room after lunch, shrieking with laughter, throwing cushions and refusing every suggestion. His mother Sonali glanced at the clock. It was long past his nap. Then he tripped, burst into tears and rubbed his eyes. She lifted him, dimmed the lights and said, "You are so tired, aren't you?" He was asleep in ten minutes.

At nine, Jomon slumped at his desk with his chin on his arm, yawning through the first period and snapping at a friend. His teacher did not send him out. They asked quietly after class, "You seem worn out. How is bedtime going, and how is the noise at home?" Jomon said the new baby next door cried half the night.

At twenty-five, Jomon made three small errors in a report and stopped laughing at meetings. His colleague Joseph found him alone at the kitchenette one afternoon. "You've seemed drained lately. Anything I can take off your plate?" Jomon let out a shaky breath.

qa.q: What did Sonali do after Jomon tripped and burst into tears?
qa.a: She lifted him, dimmed the lights and told him he was so tired.

qa.q: What do the three scenes show about how adults and colleagues can read tiredness in Jomon?
qa.a: At two a wild burst is a sign that a nap is overdue, at nine slumping and a short temper lead a teacher to ask about bedtime, and at twenty-five small mistakes lead Joseph to check in kindly, so each observer looks past the behaviour to the tiredness.

qa.q: How was Jomon probably feeling as he slumped at his desk at nine?
qa.a: Jomon was worn out and irritable, low on sleep because of the crying baby next door, which shortened his temper.

qa.q: What could a colleague do besides criticising the errors?
qa.a: A colleague can check in privately, as Joseph did, and ask what could be taken off the plate, since kindness helps more than gossip.

grounding: Sleep loss noticed by observers at three ages: a wild overtired toddler, a cheerful child now short-tempered in class, and a sharp colleague making small errors.
